content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams>: This bill would repeal Section 1502 of the Dodd-Frank Act, which directed the SEC to issue a rule (finalized in 2012) that requires public companies listed on U.S. exchanges that use ``conflict minerals'' (tin, tungsten, tantalum, and gold) from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRS) and its nine neighboring countries to carry out checks on their supply chains to determine if their purchases are fueling conflict in Congo, and to publicly report their findings. If the repeal of Section 1502 becomes law, the SEC's conflict minerals rule would be repealed as well. Repealing Section 1502's requirements, as this bill proposes, would harm investors by significantly obscuring material risk. Many investors view supply chain integrity as an important component of their investment analysis and plays an important role in their decision of whether or not to purchase a company's stock. Companies tied to human rights abuses face severe reputational damage, consumer boycotts, and potential legal liabilities; without the standardized reporting required by Section 1502, investors lose a critical, uniform dataset used to identify which companies are vulnerable to these ``off-balance-sheet'' risks. The bill's compliance costs, which Republicans and industry have long complained about, have also been significantly overestimated: Elm Sustainability Partners estimates the cost for U.S. businesses to comply with the Rule has been 74 to 85 percent less than the original SEC estimate.\1\
\1\Elm Sustainability Partners, Comment Submitted on Reconsideration of Conflict Mineral Rule Implementation (Feb. 6, 2017).
As background, the eastern portion of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has long been the site of one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. Since 1998, more than 5 million people are estimated to have died as a result of the conflict, which is ongoing. Large numbers of civilians in war-torn areas of the DRC have been the victims of horrific sexual violence, including sexual violence, mutilation, and sexual slavery carried out by armed groups. According to the GAO, in eastern DRC, armed groups that profit from exploitation of conflict minerals and other trades continue to commit severe human rights abuses.\2\
\2\GAO, Conflict Minerals: Peace and Security in Democratic Republic of the Congo Have Not Improved with SEC Disclosure Rule (GAO- 25-107018) (Oct. 7, 2024).
Recognizing the ongoing urgency of the human rights situation and the need to take action, in 2010, Congress included a provision in the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act to help break the link between the mineral trade and conflict in eastern DRC. Dodd-Frank Section 1502 provides increased supply chain transparency by requiring public companies to provide information on conflict minerals used in their products as well as their sourcing. The SEC issued a rule finalizing Section 1502's implementation in 2012.
This bill was introduced in the 115th Congress, where it received unanimous Democratic opposition at markup along with one Republican opposing. It is also opposed by the United States Sustainable Investment Forum (US SIF), the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility, and Ceres.
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 7085.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Stephen F. Lynch,
Al Green,
Bill Foster,
Joyce Beatty,
Rashida Tlaib,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Nikema Williams,
Members of Congress.
